newsitem.title: USA: NY Fed says overseas US Treasuries trade prescient.
newsitem.headline: NY Fed says overseas US Treasuries trade prescient.

text.p: Overseas price changes can effectively predict overnight price changes in New York despite lower trading volume in U.S. Treasuries in London and Tokyo, according to an analysis in the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's latest Economic Policy Review.

"Lower liquidity notwithstanding, the overseas trading locations provide important information on the path of U.S. Treasury security prices," said Michael J. Fleming, an economist in the New York Fed's capital markets area.
Fleming's "Round-the-Clock Market for U.S. Treasury Securities" provided the first detailed intraday analysis of the U.S. Treasury securities market, according to a press release from the bank.
While the Treasury market is "one of the world's largest and most liquid financial markets, there is little quantitative evidence on its intraday functioning," Fleming said.

Fleming used data on primary government securities dealers' trading activity, between April 4 and August 19, 1994, to examine trading volume, price volatility and bid-ask spreads for the three major trading locations -- New York, London and Tokyo -- and for each half-hour interval of the global trading day.

He said he found relatively low trading activity in the overseas locations as well as less price discovery -- the process by which Treasury prices adjust to incorporate new information -- and wider bid-ask spreads.

The analysis reveals that although the secondary market for U.S. Treasury securities operates around the clock, more than 94 percent of trading occcurs in New York, with less than four percent in London and less than two percent in Tokyo. Price volatility also is highly concentrated in New York trading hours (0730 EDT/1130 GMT through 1730 EDT/2130 GMT) and peaks at the same times as trading activity each day (0820 EDT/1220 GMT), the report said.

In his analysis of bid-ask spreads, Fleming determined that the spreads are higher overseas than in New York, and higher in Tokyo than in London. Spreads represent the difference between the highest price a prospective buyer will pay for a security and the lowest price a prospective seller will accept.
According to Fleming, intraday analysis of trading volume and the bid-ask spread can be used to ascertain how market liquidity changes throughout the day.

"Such information is important to hedgers and other market participants who may need to trade at any moment and to investors who rely on a liquid Treasury market for the pricing of other securities or for market tracking sentiment," Fleming said.
